questions.q: In plain JavaScript, when does calling sendTokens(42, "0.5 ETH") with swapped argument types actually cause a problem?
options: Immediately when the file is saved
Only when the code actually runs and hits the mismatched usage
At the moment the function is declared
Never — JavaScript automatically fixes swapped arguments
questions.explain: Plain JavaScript has no compile-time type checking, so a type mismatch like this only surfaces once the code actually executes.

questions.q: What does adding : string and : number type annotations to a function's parameters let TypeScript do?
options: Make the function run faster at runtime
Catch a type mismatch (like swapped arguments) at compile time, before the code ever runs
Automatically convert the arguments to the correct type
Nothing — annotations are just comments
questions.explain: TypeScript's compiler checks annotated types against how a function is actually called, flagging mismatches immediately rather than waiting for runtime.

options: A completely separate programming language unrelated to JavaScript
A superset of JavaScript — the same syntax plus optional type annotations, checked by a compiler
A JavaScript framework like React or Vue
A runtime that replaces Node.js
questions.explain: TypeScript extends JavaScript's syntax with optional types; nearly every valid JS file is already close to valid TypeScript.

questions.q: What happens to TypeScript's type annotations when the code is compiled to JavaScript?
options: They're kept in the output and checked again at runtime
They are erased entirely — the emitted .js has no trace of them
They're converted into runtime error messages
They become JSDoc comments
questions.explain: Type erasure means types only exist at compile time for checking purposes; the actual .js that runs in browsers or Node has no type information left.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue TypeScript matters especially in blockchain development?
options: Because blockchain code can't run without it
Because real funds are on the line and smart contract ABIs have many typed parameters, so catching a type mismatch before deployment matters a lot
Because Solidity requires TypeScript
Because TypeScript makes transactions execute faster on-chain
questions.explain: A wrong-type bug in code that moves real funds, or that calls a contract with many ABI-typed parameters, is far costlier to discover after deployment than before it.
